I just wanted to throw out some thoughts on Ancient Hearts for discussion.

CAVEAT: I haven't played with AH, due to the card back issue, and am
unlikely to do so in the future. However, I have read the spoilers and
the discussions of various cards.

So far, I haven't seen any outrageous spoilers. Some cards (e.g., Return
to Innocence, Scorpion Sting) may be the basis of extremely powerful
decks, but there are counters to the in the card mix, so I expect the
game can deal with it. However, a number of these card very markedly
increase the power of certain decks, e.g.:

Return to Innocence: Sneaky or otherwise unblockable bleed.
Scorpion Sting: Gangrel combat
Blood to Water: Tremere 2nd round combat
Uncontrollable Rage: Any hand-to-hand rush deck
Mass Reality: Weenie gun decks, esp. with DBR

While none of these may be spoilers per se, I think it's pretty obvious
that the above cards move the appropriate decks to entirely new levels of
power. I think the difference is marked enough that a deck without AH
will generally have a poor chance in an environment with substantial AH.

In other words, WotC is escalating the game (intentionally or not).

This doesn't appear limited to Magic. Consider the ad for the new Magic
expansion I saw on the back of the last Inquest:

>>>>>>>>>>>
ALLIANCES

PLAY TO WIN

(picture of ongoing Magic game)

(picture of cheery teenager)

"Hey, check out this card!"

(picture of dejected teenager obvious playing with Cheery)

"What the ^&%$^*%$&!"

(Cheery)

"It's awesome!"

(Dejected)

"Game over, man."
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>

They're obviously implying that you need cards from Alliances to stay
competitive (as well as obviously marketing to the munchkins). A good
friend of mine who still plays Magic says that the situation with
Alliances resembles that of AH - there's no out-and-out spoilers, but a
lot of cards that markedly increase the power level. He thinks he will
have to rebuild every single one of his decks to keep up.

Anyway, I think I detect a shift in strategy from WotC. For quite some
time, they've been trying to despoiler Magic and keep the power level
under control. I think the relatively low average power level of Dark
Sovereigns implies that was the strategy there as well, and the
high-powered cards from DS were inadequately playtested errors. This
contrasts with AH and Alliances, which both have lots of high-powered, but
relatively well-tested cards. I believe the relative disappointments of
Homelands and DS, and the realization that the munchkin market is quite a
bit bigger than the serious gamer market, have convinced WotC that they
will sell more cards (and make more $$$) with mild to moderate escalation
in new expansions.

Curt Adams (curt...@aol.com)

I must disagree with your point about "Power Escalation" in AH, as most of
the cards I have seen that seem to increase power actually only patch
holes in the game propper. Take for instance the cards Scorpion Sting and
Blood to Water.

Scorpion Sting aids the Gangrel greatly, but only against decks that up
till now they were completely (and unfairly) useless against. Before
Scorpion Sting (and Dog Pack), even the most efficient and killer Gangrel
combat deck was completely helpless against a deck that was outfitted with
a handfull of S:CE or Dodges. A dozen Majesties or Nimble Feet in a deck
would completely negate the use of even the best Gangrel deck. With
Scorpion Sting and Dog Pack, the Gangrel can fight well against combat
avoidance decks, which is as it should be. Combat decks should be able to
compete on even ground with Bleed and Vote decks, and up until now, has
not been the case. Now the Gangrel can compete on an even level against
these decks, which before they could do nothing against. Scorpion Sting
has no effect against other non combat-avoidance decks, or Fortitude
decks, so fails to break the game there, and basically patches a big hole
in the Gangrel deck that should not have been there to begin with. Dog
Pack prevents S:CE, and S:CE is pretty much agreed to be more potent than
it should be.

Blood to Water, while it seems pretty grusome, only helps if the Tremere
can make it a second round of combat. Now, if they do, they will REALLY
kill you, but that is the way it is supposed to be, and before now, was
just not the case. Even if the Tremere managed to make it alive to a
second round (all the dodges and Theft of Vitae in the world won't help
the Tremere against Immortal Grapple or, well, Scorpion Sting), their
mighty Cauldron of Blood/Drain Vitae/Walk of Flame strikes could still be
Dodged or S:CE or Prevented(for the ones you can prevent). The Tremere "I
kill you on the second round" deck has never been as scary as it should
be, and now at least if they make it that far, they can do 5 unpreventable
damage before you Dodge/S:CE/Fortitude their huge killer strike. Granted,
with Thoughts Betrayed, the Tremere can become mighty scary, but IMHO
Thoughts Betrayed is a VERY broken card (the only broken card I can think
of out of DS), where Blood to Water has almost the same effect (makes the
Tremere as good as they should be) but is not even close to as offensive
as TB.

Yes, certain decks that are built without AH cards will not be as good as
those same decks with AH cards, but that is mostly because the AH cards
help to patch holes in the basic game design, not because the AH cards are
particularly killer cards.

pd...@aol.com (PDB6) writes

"I must disagree with your point about "Power Escalation" in AH, as
most of the cards I have seen that seem to increase power actually only
patch holes in the game propper. Take for instance the cards Scorpion
Sting and Blood to Water. "

You're not contesting my claim that AH escalates the power level of Jyhad.
You even specifically state that it drastically rasises the power level
of a couple of decks. Yor disagree in that you say this was an
appropriate and necessary escalation rather than (as I claim) a
market-driven or accidental escalation. We don't disagree on the effect,
merely on the motivation.

Obviously neither of us has access to the thought processes of the AH
designers, so there's no way to resolve the disagreement directly. They
themselves may not even know why they changed the power level - sometimes
people do things without clearly understaning why. I can however, argue
that the original power level of your example clans was not a flaw, but
typified what I believe is an excellent aspect of Jyhad.

You complain that it was possible to make any deck nearly immune to
Gangrel or Tremere with a good supply of defensive combat cards. This is
indeed true, but it's nearly universally true of ANY Jyhad deck. It's
likewise possible to be nearly immune to any strategy - bleed bounce or
rush for S&B, Delaying tactics or intercept for vote, etc. This is a very
good thing, as you rarely get the "ah, nothing I can do" problem you see
with most CCGs, and you can play almost any clan in any environment just
by adjusting your card mix.

This defensive flexibility didn't cause problems with unbeatable decks, as
building a deck to ignore Gangrel entailed 20-25% defensive combat cards.
If you played between 2 non-combat decks you spent the game staring at an
endless hand jam of Dodge and Press to End.

Now a few things stood out from this system. Celerity combat definitely
broke the rules, as there was no defense against additional strikes save
combat ends or outrageous amounts of fortitude (or Celerity of your own).
Tremere, Malks, and Nosferatu were all pretty much helpless before Cel/Pot
or Celerity gun decks. But THIS was the problem, not the manageable power
level of more reasonable combat decks.

WotC seems to be raising all the combat clans to the semi-spoilerish level
of Celerity combat. Certainly with the AH and DS cards "normal" combat
defense is basically useless against Brujah, Tremere, or Gangrel. Given
that WotC won't withdraw cards, or errata them weaker, perhaps this was
the only way to deal with the relative imbalance of Celerity vs. other
combat strategies. But there are 2 big problems.

First, it creates a planned obsolesence problem in that it requires
ongoing card purchases to keep up with the escalating power level. We
can't say "just buy a few starters, trade, and you're set indefinitely".
Now to invite someone into V:tES we must honestly tell them they will have
to keep buying more cards as long as WotC keeps printing expansions.

Second, it shortcircuits the old Jyhad game's defense against excessively
powerful strategies. In old Jyhad, if one strategy turned out too good,
everyone increased the proportion of defense vs. that strategy and the
game rolled on without loss of variety or strategies. Against combat,
Malks would put in dodges, Tremere maneuvers, Ventrue Fortitude damage
prevention, etc. The game had a resiliency in that it could survive even
fairly substantial playtesting errors. With this new power level it ain't
so. If Gangrel Rush turns out too strong with Uncontrollable
Rage/Scorpion Sting/Dog Pack, the game variety will abruptly collapse into
the few decks that can cope with that kind of thing.

FWIW, my group finds Gangrel to be perfectly playable, and quite strong,
with the original card set. Tremere combat is a bit weak, but this is
compensated for with the flexibility from Auspex intercept, Dominate
Bleed, and extensive bleed bounce.

Curt Adams (curt...@aol.com)

Well, I guess one man's "Power Escalation" is on man's "Play Balance".
You say tomato, I say tomato (that just doesn't translate into print real
well, does it :-)

The cards in AH, I found, mostly fix up what I had found to be problems in
the game. They were not huge problems, and the fixes are not huge fixes.
Mostly, I have noticed that the cards in AH have helped put the combat
deck up to par with the bleed deck and the vote deck. While this could
grow into a completely different thread, in my experience combat decks,
while viable, are much more difficult to make work than either of the
other two basic deck designs. Firstly, combat's mean to the basic end
(reducing its preys pool to zero) is incredibly obtuse and card combo
intensive (as opposed to S&B or KRC). Secondly, the amount of effort
needed to counteract a combat deck is much lesser than the effort needed
to make a combat deck work, i.e. an ounce of combat avoidance is worth a
pound of combat. Mind you, this is not something I wish to debate, this
is just something our gaming group has discovered over the last year of
playing Jyhad. At the Origin's Jyhad game last year and a half (the only
non-local Jyhad experience I have had), out of the 20 or so decks I saw
myself and the other 20 or so decks that were seen by my cohort, we saw
only 1 combat deck, and that was some "Zip Gun/Dragon Breath Round"
monstrosity that I don't even consider a honest combat deck. I don't know
if this was a result of a problem, or a symptom of a problem, but there it
was.

All the problems you pointed out about celerity, I basically agree with,
but there have always been good ways to deal with celerity, be it sending
them to torpor before they get to use their additional strikes or playing
with Skin of Steel. The Nosferatu (or other Brujah) could always get away
with Immortal Grapple and big hits, hoping that the Brujah was relying on
Blur rather than stacked Potence strikes but the Gangrel could do nothing
but try to not die as they Dodge and multi-strike. The Tremere never have
been as good at combat as they could have been, which is indeed made up
for by their versatility, but it would be nice to be able to make a
Tremere deck that could fight effectively.

I guess, all in all, I agree with WOTCs development of the game. At some
point they realized that Sneak and Bleed was too easy to get away with,
and so they added stuff to fix that. I guess now they have realized what
I have known all along, that combat was too difficult to make work
(relative to voting or bleeding), so thay have added stuff to fix that.

I am viewing the release of AH trough the eyes of a player in a group that
has evolved the combat deck to an art form, and in doing so, have found
all the big (and small) flaws with the various clans on that level. AH,
we have found, patched these up and made us happy.

Jyhad is still a game where you can buy a couple of starters, a hand full
of boosters and play with, but in that enviornment, you will end up with a
bunch of people playing Malk S&B decks. Then everyone will want to buy
more cards to try to deal with that and work from there. If they go out
and buy some AH, more power to them :-)

CurtAdams <curt...@aol.com> wrote:

Then you'll forgive me for ignoring any comments you have on the power
level of the cards in general. The only sure way to know how powerful
a card is is to play with it; eyeballing it normally isn't enough.

>In other words, WotC is escalating the game (intentionally or not).

So you say. But you've just said you aren't even going to play with the
cards, so how would you know?

>They're obviously implying that you need cards from Alliances to stay

>Alliances resembles that of AH - there's no out-and-out spoilers, but a
>lot of cards that markedly increase the power level. He thinks he will
>have to rebuild every single one of his decks to keep up.

A gross overstatement. Various decks will want to retune themselves to
account for Alliances cards, but this is true for any expansion. New
cards shake things up, and it's insane to think that the typical deck can
keep up its level of performance if it doesn't change. But this has to do
more with flexibility and such than with sheer power.

>Anyway, I think I detect a shift in strategy from WotC. For quite some
>time, they've been trying to despoiler Magic and keep the power level
>under control. I think the relatively low average power level of Dark
>Sovereigns implies that was the strategy there as well, and the
>high-powered cards from DS were inadequately playtested errors. This
>contrasts with AH and Alliances, which both have lots of high-powered, but
>relatively well-tested cards. I believe the relative disappointments of
>Homelands and DS, and the realization that the munchkin market is quite a
>bit bigger than the serious gamer market, have convinced WotC that they
>will sell more cards (and make more $$$) with mild to moderate escalation
>in new expansions.

Dark Sovereigns was the first expansion for V:TES, and we played it a bit
conservatively since it was unclear what the impact of an expansion would be.
While it is true that the average card power is ramping up slightly, this is
not aimed at catering to the munchkins. A weak card set is a boring card set;
I doubt that even a fourth of the Fourth Edition card set is used tournaments,
for example, and one would think that more like a third of the basic set
would appear in tournaments. Also, if we stop printing "wallpaper" cards,
which everyone seems to be in favor of, then the power level will escalate
by definition.

It was recognized early on that a trading card game can't help but escalate
slightly over time, as new cards make existing strategies slightly more
efficient, unless the designers actively try to tone things down. What we
don't want is for the power level to be making quantum jumps following the
release of an expansion, which I don't think has happened with either
Ancient Hearts or Alliances.

My primary initial claim, that many Jyhad deck are much more powerful with

only applies to decks shortchanged by the previous cardset, but neither of
you is disagreeing with the change in power.

>Various decks will want to retune themselves to account for

>shake things up, and it's insane to think that the typical deck
>can keep up its level of performance if it doesn't change. But
>this has to do more with flexibility and such than with sheer >power.

New V:tES cards needn't alter the balance of power. 3 options:

1) New cards are only those applying to the new clans, plus a few obvious
missing links (like adoption and Clan Impersonation). This would expand
the game without any meaningful change in power level.

2) New cards apply to existing clans, but provide no impartant new
abilities. This would create your situation where increased power comes
only from flexibility and not raw card power

3) New cards provide important new abilities to existing decks and clans.
This obviously does increase the power level.

AH is clearly class 3. Giving Gangrel and Tremere ways to ignore Dodge is
definitely an important new ability. Including vampires with extensive
out-of-clan abilities is definitely an important new ability. Giving a
non-stealth clan (Tremere) 2 vampires with built-in stealth is definitely
an important new ability. Cards that produce major global benefits (like
Mass Reality) are definitely an important new ability.

Tom Wylie writes:

>Also, if we stop printing "wallpaper" cards, which
>everyone seems to be in favor of, then the power level
>will escalate by definition.

Not if you follow option 1 above. But do stop wallpaper as much as you
can, regardless of your choice of expansion power level; even a smaller
set is better if no purchasing is wasted on filling up closets.

>A weak card set is a boring card set. It was recognized early on

>that a trading card game can't help but escalate slightly over
>time, as new cards make existing strategies slightly more
>efficient, unless the designers actively try to tone things down.
>What we don't want is for the power level to be making quantum
>jumps following the release of an expansion, which I don't think
>has happened with either Ancient Hearts or Alliances.

Sorry if this came across as an attack. Escalation is common in
sequential fiction - people tend to lose interest in a story which is
continually more of the same. I understand that commercial pressures may
force WotC (or any other CCG manufacturer) to do the same with their CCGs.
CCGs do share some aspects of sequential fiction. But AH was escalated
more than game considerations would require (class 3 versus class 1 or
even class 2). Your comments about "weak card sets" indicates this was
intentional, not accidental. Although I cannot say what WotC's intentions
were, that Inquest ad inclines me to suspect that the intent was to please
the munchkin market (the actual escalation itself gives no clear
indication). I acknowledge that the reason could have been a desire for a
certain turnover rate in tournament deck construction, a response to
customer surveys, or any of a number of other items.

I am not sure where you get "no _important_ new abilities"==boring. The

expansion. Neither did Ravnos. What they did get was more versatility
and things that added in with their current strategies. Far from boring.

is immaterial.

To add to Curt's statement, these abilities would be something that really

with increase in cost, escalation comes in.

> >non-stealth clan (Tremere) 2 vampires with built-in stealth is definitely
> >an important new ability. Cards that produce major global benefits (like
> >Mass Reality) are definitely an important new ability.

While I disagree with Curt on Mass Reality, he is correct about the new
Tremere +1 stealther. With two of them, the Tremere are given a totally
new power.

> All of the above is true, but these are the sorts of things that make
> expansions interesting: new abilities, not boring rehashes.

By important new abilities, I mean giving typical clan powers or
disciplines things that are not in line with what they were able to do
before. In my mind, it shouldn't happen. There are certain things that
Fortitude cannot do, there are certain things that don't make sense for
Brujah, etc.. In a game mechanics sense, new powers should happen, but
their cost is important.

I didn't see AH as a boring rehash, and for the most part, no old thing
got any new abilities (two exceptions: Gangrel combat and Tremere
stealth). Their existing abilities were expanded or if their abilities
were focused (Blood to Water, for example), ample cost was made on the
cards. I hope to see this continue, but I am wary (given your responses)
that I might see escalation in the Sabbat (meaning increase focus of
already existing strategies without appropriate cost (making game balance
harder to coordinate as the card set increases)).

expansion. I believe that upping the power of already viable decks will
decrease, not increase, variety.
>Part of the

>whole *point* of expansions is to shake things up a bit, so people

Wouldn't it then be better to introduce cards that permit new deck types

power of existing decks? Making existing mainstream decks stronger, if
anything, reduces the variety of existing decks. (The cards I mentioned
all help existing already-viable decks) The cards that give Gangrel

vampires with Quietus. To use a new discipline will require a radical
change in both crypt and library; it would be a new deck.

>In other words, the new decks would be boring since they could have been

games
>that are played with card limits anyway, since people can play with more
>action modifiers that provide stealth, or with a tighter set of combat
>strikes, or what have you.

Well, since existing decks aren't boring, the new ones wouldn't be either.
In addition, you would see at the very least major variations on existing
themes, and probably whole new possibilities. For example, just adding
some small vampires with Thaumaturgy might make a Cryptic Mission deck
functional. A few Thaumaturgy actions could add a lot of variety to such
a deck, too. These actions don't need to be able to burn a vampire or add

useful; indeed such powers would be rather detrimental.

Wake, Blood Doll, Telepathic Counter, Fake Out, etc. Card limit games
would be much more like no-limit games as you could use adequate numbers

mine sits on the shelf as I haven't enough Blood Dolls and Wakes.

Messages.Author: The Corrupter
Messages.Body:
On Mon, 8 Jul 1996, Bastet wrote:

[Re: Indomitability vs. Hidden Strength]

> But Hidden strength costs way too much and effectively only blocks one
> point. Though, I admit there are a few (VERY few) uses for hidden
> strength it is little more than wallpaper.

Actually, most people I know say that Hidden Strength made Indomitability
wallpaper. In actuality, they both have their place.
Indomitability:
Inf: Prevent 1 damage
Sup: Press, or Prevent 1 damage with Optional Press
Hidden Strength:
Inf: X Blood to prevent X+1 damage
Sup: as above with an optional press

Hidden Strength is effectively preventing the loss of just as much blood
as Indomitability, but can stop aggravated from meaning anything.
However, it is more flexible (and cheaper) than Skin of Steel, when you
want to prevent small amounts of damage (say 1) or retainer damage.
However, unlike Indomitability, you cannot use Hidden Strength's press
unless you have prevented damage.

Each card does something useful.

Messages.Author: DOUGDWISE
Messages.Body:
For The Corrupter, Peter, and Tom:
Yes, I too think that there was a slight escalation in power with the AH
expansion and that some of the cards aided strategies that really didn't
need the help. The Tremere got another Vampire with permanent stealth (
huh?) and the Gangrel got some additional strikes (so why play celerity?)
I agree that the apparent weakness of the Gangrel deck to celerity combat
decks was not a major problem. No combat deck should be perfect. Every
deck design, combat or other, should have to weigh trade-offs and balance
benefits with weaknesses. If I have those dodges in my hand during
combat, I have given something else up that I could have in that card
slot. I am not, however, unhappy with the AH card set in general. I
actually like the set and think that it is quite well done.
Yes, I do think the AH expansion adds a lot to the play environment. I
don't think there was any burning need for the Gangrel to get additional
strikes (where did that come from?) but the Dog Pack doesn't bother me. I
think it is so expensive and fragile (and limitted to one vamp) that it
won't be a big factor in play. The Tremere won't be much better at combat
than they are now with their Blood To Water. They have a devil of a time
getting to the second round, but if they do manage to press they will be a
bit better off.
Tom, I think AH is really quite good. Certainly there are things I would
change, but you guys did a pretty good job. No major complaints from my
keyboard about the set. I may revise that opinion after some more playing
( I plan to try some Assamite combat) but any thoughts about the set will
be presented as constructive suggestions rather than whining ( no offense
intended to _anyone_.) Good work, Tom, I think you guys can be proud.
Also, the cards seem to be much sturdier and resilient. (I missed you at
the San Diego Comic Con this weekend. Wanted to tell you in person how
much I appreciate your efforts on the newsgroup and in the Duelist.)
Hope everybody will try this expansion and find something they like in it.
Thanks for listening.
Doug Dunaway
